metadata.title: Wall Street Futures Rise as Nasdaq Attempts Recovery Following Three-Month Lows: Dow Jones, S&P, Nasdaq

content.text:
US stock index futures pointed to a higher opening on Tuesday as investors looked for opportunities to buy technology shares following another sharp market decline. Nasdaq 100 futures advanced 0.8%, despite a substantial premarket drop in Apple shares, while fluctuating oil prices and stronger-than-expected US manufacturing data remained in focus.
The anticipated rebound followed a difficult Monday session in which the Nasdaq and S&P 500 reversed early gains to close at their lowest levels in three months. Concerns about the outlook for artificial intelligence continued to weigh on technology stocks, while falling crude oil prices triggered significant losses across the energy sector.
Nasdaq Futures Advance Despite Sharp Decline in Apple Shares
Nasdaq 100 futures rose 0.8% ahead of Tuesday's opening bell, suggesting renewed buying interest following the technology sector's recent selloff.
The advance came despite a 4.4% decline in premarket trading for Apple (NASDAQ:AAPL), after the iPhone manufacturer reported quarterly results that raised concerns about future profitability.
Apple recorded higher revenue and earnings but forecast a gross margin for the current quarter slightly below analyst expectations.
The company attributed the weaker-than-anticipated outlook to increasing component prices, highlighting growing cost pressures affecting its hardware business.
The announcement added to uncertainty surrounding technology shares, which have already faced significant selling pressure in recent sessions.
Nevertheless, the positive movement in Nasdaq futures suggested that some investors were seeking buying opportunities following the market's recent declines.
Nasdaq and S&P 500 Close at Three-Month Lows
Wall Street experienced a volatile trading session on Monday, with major indices initially advancing before reversing direction.
The Nasdaq Composite fell 272.68 points, or 1.1%, to close at 25,164.32.
The S&P 500 declined 38.67 points, or 0.5%, to finish at 7,541.40.
Both indices extended the losses recorded during the previous Thursday and Friday sessions, reaching their lowest closing levels in three months.
The reversal reflected continued weakness in technology shares and renewed concerns about the outlook for artificial intelligence-related investments.
Although bargain hunting initially supported the market, selling pressure intensified as the session progressed, erasing early gains.
Dow Jones Advances as Consumer and Industrial Stocks Gain
Unlike the Nasdaq and S&P 500, the Dow Jones Industrial Average managed to finish Monday's session in positive territory.
The index gained 213.67 points, or 0.4%, closing at 51,983.98.
Strong performances from Sherwin-Williams (NYSE:SHW), Home Depot (NYSE:HD) and Walmart (NYSE:WMT) helped support the blue-chip benchmark.
The divergence between the Dow and the technology-heavy Nasdaq highlighted differences in performance across major sectors.
While technology stocks faced substantial selling pressure, gains in selected consumer and industrial companies provided support for the narrower Dow index.
The contrasting movements demonstrated that the market downturn was particularly concentrated in technology and energy shares.
Technology Stocks Slide as AI Concerns Persist
Technology shares remained among the weakest performers during Monday's session as investors continued reassessing the outlook for artificial intelligence.
Computer hardware stocks experienced particularly heavy selling, with the NYSE Arca Computer Hardware Index plunging 5.5%.
The decline pushed the index to its lowest closing level in three months.
Semiconductor, networking and software companies also recorded substantial losses.
The broad weakness reflected continued uncertainty surrounding AI-related investment expectations and the potential implications for technology sector valuations.
The declines contributed significantly to the Nasdaq's retreat and reinforced concerns about the sustainability of the sector's recent performance.
Tuesday's positive futures movement suggested a possible recovery attempt, although Apple's disappointing margin outlook remained a source of pressure.
Energy Stocks Plunge as Oil Prices Fall More Than 7%
Energy shares also suffered significant losses on Monday as crude oil prices declined sharply.
US crude oil futures fell more than 7%, dropping well below $100 per barrel.
The selloff followed renewed optimism that diplomatic negotiations could lead to a resolution of the ongoing conflict between the United States and Iran.
Lower oil prices weighed heavily on energy companies, with the Philadelphia Oil Service Index declining 5.1%.
The NYSE Arca Oil Index also fell sharply, losing 4.3%.
The declines reflected concerns that a sustained reduction in crude prices could weaken revenue and profitability across parts of the energy industry.
At the same time, lower energy costs offered potential relief for other sectors facing inflationary and operating cost pressures.
US-Iran Diplomatic Efforts Influence Oil Markets
Developments in the Middle East remained a major influence on energy prices and broader market sentiment.
Over the weekend, US Secretary of State Marco Rubio indicated that President Donald Trump preferred a diplomatic resolution to the conflict with Iran.
Rubio said the administration remained confident in its military capabilities but favoured a peaceful outcome.
"What the president expresses to you is incredible confidence that if we needed to do something militarily, we would have the ability to do it, and we really we have everything we need to be successful," Rubio said.
"But we would prefer to do it peacefully."
Discussions involving Iranian officials and Qatari mediators also contributed to expectations of a possible diplomatic breakthrough.
The prospect of reduced geopolitical tensions encouraged selling in crude oil markets as investors reassessed potential supply disruptions.
Oil prices initially rebounded on Tuesday before US crude futures moved firmly back into negative territory during the morning.
The continued volatility highlighted the sensitivity of energy markets to developments in diplomatic negotiations.
US Manufacturing Activity Expands More Than Expected
Economic data provided a more positive signal for the US economy after the Institute for Supply Management reported stronger-than-expected manufacturing activity in October.
The ISM Manufacturing Purchasing Managers' Index increased to 55.5 from 54.5 in September.
Economists had expected a more modest rise to 54.6.
A reading above 50 indicates expansion in manufacturing activity, meaning the latest figure pointed to continued growth in the sector.
The increase also suggested that manufacturing conditions improved more significantly than analysts had anticipated.
The stronger data provided additional information for investors assessing the resilience of the US economy amid financial market volatility.
Investors Assess Technology Weakness and Oil Price Volatility
Tuesday's positive futures performance suggested that Wall Street could attempt another recovery following three consecutive sessions of pressure on the Nasdaq and S&P 500.
Technology stocks remained central to market sentiment, particularly after Apple's weaker-than-expected gross margin guidance and the previous session's sharp decline in computer hardware shares.
Meanwhile, fluctuating crude oil prices continued to reflect changing expectations surrounding diplomatic efforts to resolve the US-Iran conflict.
Stronger manufacturing data offered some support for the economic outlook, with the ISM index rising to 55.5 in October.
Investors will be watching whether early buying interest can be sustained after Monday's reversal, when initial gains gave way to significant losses in technology and energy shares.
